utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated, have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First I would like to say good afternoon to the interpreters and to our translators. Of course, good afternoon to the counsel, as well. We have a great many documents here. Before we with the cross-examination of General Marin, we would have the witness brought in first. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, I do hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sure that counsel already told you, we're now going to give the floor to the Prosecution, that is to Mr. Kehoe, but we want to remind you that you are still under oath. And now we can begin with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, we have not been formally introduced, but we have been standing here for some time around the charts here. My name is Greg Kehoe, to my right is my colleague, Mark Harmon, and to his right, the handsome young chap to his right is Andrew Cayley. So if I may, I would like to ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suppose Mr. Harmon is also a handsome young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He's in an advanced state of deterioration, like I am, Judge, so I don't put him in the same category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, I would like to ask you some questions about your testimony over the past week or so, and I would like to start, if I could, on your background. Take us back a little bit and tell the Court and the rest of us a little bit about your education, if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I completed elementary school in Novi Travnik, secondary school also in Novi Travnik. I graduated from the faculty of political sciences, the department for social work and the department of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the last bit of education that you just talked to us about, that you graduated from the department of defence; what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former state, that is the former Yugoslavia, at the faculty of political sciences, there was a department which was headed defence. In that department people were trained, the people who wanted to study the subject, were trained to work in headquarters, in civilian defence matters, and to work in former headquarters of the Territorial Defence. Also, they could find employment in secondary schools teaching young people to prepare for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, what subject or what area did you study in the department of defence in the university?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the framework of that faculty, upon graduation, one acquired the title of professor. So, I became professor of defence, and I could apply to work in a secondary school or in other civilian institutions dealing with defence within the former structure of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this defence, this degree from the department of the defence, was it of some value to the former Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably it was. Upon graduation from this university department, according to the former law and education, you required a university degree. If the need existed and there was a competition announced, then people with these qualifications could apply for a position in the former Yugoslav People's Army; but it didn't necessarily mean that you would be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was while I was doing my regular military service. I said in my introduction that I did my military service in the school for officers in reserve. I spent six months there, and after that, another six months of military service; and when I completed that service I had the rank of reserve sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about the JNA, just very briefly, Brigadier. Since you studied it at some detail in the university, I think you could be helpful to us. You noted during the course of your examination that Blaskic only had three officers in his headquarters that had graduated from the military academy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And those three officers were himself, I believe -- who were they, himself and who were the other two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to give you their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I would, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic, Ivica Zeko, Mijo Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your opinion, were these three officers very well-trained officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were young officers. They didn't have sufficient experience to carry out the tasks they were assigned in the HVO, because before they joined the HVO they were at the level of a company, or perhaps some auxiliary positions in a unit of brigade level. I don't know what positions these colleagues of mine had in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But they graduated from the military academy prior to -- they graduated from the military academy and they were officers in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how else did you become an officer in the JNA, other than going to the military academy? I'm talking about being an active service officer; how else could you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this is quite correct, what I'm going to say, because after all, it was a long time ago. I think you could have graduated from a higher school, and I am not familiar with all the preconditions required to become an officer; but as far as I know, those officers could not have any duties above the level of a platoon or a company. I'm not quite sure of all that I have just said, because all of this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when did the JNA stop conscription?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please specify this question? Because conscription in the former army occurred at two levels. So, what exactly do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It may be my terms, Brigadier, were imprecise; but when was national service abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me, I'm afraid, but I'll try and answer it to the best of my ability. Are you asking me when the JNA ceased calling up young people for military service? Because there was a rule that all young men had to do their military service. Or do you mean when young people ceased to enrol at military academies and military schools?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did the JNA cease calling up people for military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA did not cease calling up people, as far as I know. As far as I know, young people didn't wish to go to the JNA after the aggression against the Republic of Slovenia, and this was even more widespread after the aggression of the JNA against Croatia and later Bosnia and Herzegovina; but I couldn't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, would it be fair to say that people stopped going to the JNA sometime in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you talked about officers that went to the military academy, and you also refer to the fact that there were reserve officers, and that you had gone to reserve officer's training. Now, explain that to the Judges, if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school for reserve officers, in the former armed forces, because that is what they were called, the armed forces consisted of the former JNA and the Territorial Defence; and this school trained officers so that after an additional period of practical training and certain courses and exercises, they could be in command of units at the level of a company. That was the purpose of the school for reserve officers. It existed for all branches and services; infantry, artillery, communications, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How long did these reserve officers train for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already said, I spent six months in this school, and after that I went, joined the troops for practical training, and at the time I was deputy commander of the platoon. After six or seven months spent there, I returned home and continued to do my regular civilian jobs. That applied to all people who completed, who graduated from this school of reserve officers at the end of their military service. This was part of their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, between the training and the actual work with the platoons, you, as a reserve officer, had a year's training in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not training. I had six months of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You had a year's active service between your training and your work with the platoons in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this wasn't active service, I was doing my military service. It was an obligation in the former state, and this military service meant an obligation on all able-bodied men in the period from 18 to 26 years of age. They had to do their military service. Which branch or service they would go to, this was determined by recruitment commissions, and depending on the needs of the former army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in any event, you will agree with me, Brigadier, you were in the JNA for a year, or approximately a year; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the JNA for a year doing my regular military service, like any other citizen of appropriate age in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the reserve officer system, was that an intricate part of the JNA defence structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the JNA relied on the reserve officers, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In its organisation the former Yugoslav People's Army had units which were under the command of reserve officers in some cases; but the level of that unit could not be higher than a company. In some conditions those officers could be deputy commanders of battalions, but they couldn't go higher up in the chain of command, because they were not trained for that, and they were not trained on a daily basis for executing such jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, in addition to having active service officers, such as the accused, Blaskic, the JNA had reserve officers, and they also had the structure of national service, as you noted, national service by every male between 18 and 26; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the age group you were mentioning, between 18 and 26, you had to go and do your national service, and then when you returned, you were still under obligation to be called up until, I think, you were 60, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This system that was set up by the JNA of the active officers, the reserve officers, national service by every male between 18 and 26, was tied to the concept of a total national defence; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a concept of defence prepared and organised by the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This total national defence, in addition to incorporating the JNA active and reserve officers, also incorporated the Territorial Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This Territorial Defence, why don't you explain to the Judges -- you were educated in this -- explain what the Territorial Defence was in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia was a segment of the armed forces which were developed in the former Yugoslavia. They were less well armed units than the Yugoslav People's Army, and these were units, as far as I can recall, with a different assignment from those of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what was the theory, the military theory of the integration between the JNA and the Territorial Defence should hostilities break out by some outside aggressor, such as the then Soviet Union? What was the theory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, within the defence structure of the former Yugoslavia constituted the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia. In the event of aggression against the former Yugoslavia there were different concepts regarding the use and deployment of these forces. In order to clarify my answer to your question, in practice, it would be as follows: If an aggression were to occur against a certain territory, all units of the Territorial Defence in that area would be subordinated to the highest command of the Yugoslav People's Army whose zone of responsibility that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, what you're telling the Court, and correct me if I'm wrong, is that in the time of an aggression, the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defences would work in concert, work together with the Territorial Defences being subordinated to the JNA command structure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly, yes. That is right. But in practice the Yugoslav People's Army had the duty to take upon itself the initial strike of any possible aggression against the former state; and following mobilisation of reserve forces, then the Territorial Defence would also join in that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as the name indicates, the Territorial Defence was a geographically based unit; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Its organisation went as far as the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this system, being geographically based, this Territorial Defence system working in concert with the JNA, was a system that the former Yugoslavia depended on and relied on for almost 50 years; isn't that right? 45 years, 50 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Only in those 45 or 50 years there were various organisational changes that took place. Because this organisation that we have been discussing didn't exist immediately, 1945 or 1950 that is, from 1945 until 1990 the defence system was adjusted and improved, according to the views of military experts in those days, for it to be able to successfully defend itself against possible aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no doubt you know more about the structure than I do, but correct me if I'm wrong; suffice it to say that the Territorial Defence system that was an integral part of the defence system of the former Yugoslavia, was territoriality based until the fall of the former Yugoslavia. I'm talking about the collapse of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly that is true. But I said that the Territorial Defence, its organisation and structure ended at the republic level. After the JNA collapsed, the republics retained the Territorial Defence as the initial form of their organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That initial form of the organisation was the foundation for a defence system within Bosnia, for instance, that ultimately led to the HVO or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That couldn't be put quite like that, because the Territorial Defence was, for many military conscripts, synonymous with the Yugoslav People's Army; so that people did not gladly accept or look upon favourably the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, were you in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From when to when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: '95, '96. No, I'm sorry, I apologise, '85, '86.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was in Pucarevo, or what was Pucarevo or Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Novi Travnik. I worked in the department for organisation and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your section of the Territorial Defence was focused around the municipality of Novi Travnik; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's change subjects here, Brigadier, and I would like to talk to you just a little bit about some of your comments about the Central Bosnian Operative Zone and your comparisons to the NATO charts. I believe those were Defence exhibits that we had before. If we could turn to those exhibits briefly, and I believe that is 248, Defence 248. Do you have those charts, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, where do those charts come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This chart was part of the preparatory material which we are now using in the federation army and on the basis of this material, such as the one I have in my hand, we organise the district staffs and corps staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, can you tell me the name of this manual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, maybe it's FM 105, but to be very specific, this is the material which MPRI is using for the federation army with the objective of establishing the corps and district staffs headquarters. This is what we're doing in the federation army, and this is how a district or a corps of which I am a chief of staff is going to look. This is maybe 90 per cent of how it's going to look like and because I am dealing with it, I know of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this is not a NATO document, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document reflects a structure of a corps or a district in NATO. However, there is also a different structure of certain different corps based on its purpose, based on its use. Because the NATO system is used throughout the world and for us, for the purposes of the federation army, we were offered the things that were the most rational, the most appropriate for our needs in case we are attacked and we needed to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me see if I understand you correctly. During your testimony, did you equate the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to a NATO corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the Operative Zone, that is its command, had that level, was of that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you have any armoured divisions in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we never had armoured divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have any air transport, such as helicopters? Any air transport like that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many intelligence Brigades did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many artillery Brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many engineering Brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have any cavalry Brigades or divisions in the corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, I just read to you the United States 7th corps that went to the Gulf War in 1991, which had conservatively on the low end 100.000 soldiers in the corps. Now according to the testimony -- you know Ivica Zecko, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ivica Zecko told us, and this is on page 11717, in response to a question and then a follow up question by Judge Riad asking how many soldiers were in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. He noted that there were 8.000 to 8.200, and I just read you the 7th US Corps with conservatively 100,000 troops. Now, you would agree with me, would you not, sir, that there is a discrepancy between those numbers of some significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference in numbers. However, in the organisation of a military of the BH army, in conditions of this kind, what we had at our disposal were the infantry forces. Let me try to clarify this point further for you; in the structure and the name of a particular district, it can be a Brigade. It can have an armoured division or Brigade. It may have artillery Brigades. It may have a significant reconnaissance forces. It all depends on the purpose of this particular military organisation. If this military organisation is meant for tactical operations it would have a particular organisation, and this organisation, however, will depend on the resources and equipment. Even to date, in this organisation, we did not have the forces which you have just mentioned, armoured divisions, et cetera, and so on. This does not exist even in a BH army, which is now developing three corps. So these are corps or these are districts or organisations which have what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, but the bottom line, Brigadier, is your comparison of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to a NATO corps is inaccurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my understanding, the way I understand the issues, and in order to present to the Trial Chamber the organisation which was supposed to be in place and which we actually had, I took this as an example and I thought that it was quite a vivid example regarding the organisation and structure of our Operative Zone command. Because when this structure was defined for the federation army, which we have been building now, if we take into account the beginnings of the HVO and HVO army since 1992, even to date, we do not have the forces which you have mentioned, including air transport. But we are calling it a district. We are calling it an organisation. We have a territory. We have a population. For the needs of the defence of the federation, if somebody should start an aggression against us, these are the forces which we will defend ourselves with. You can have a weak organisation or a strong organisation, but an organisation is an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, my learned friend, Mr. Nobilo, asked you whether or not you were regularly in touch with NATO experts and that's at page 12065, to which you responded in the affirmative. Was your answer to his question on that subject in the affirmative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when you talk about the structure, the definition of structure, about the build up of this organisation, I am in touch with the MPRI experts. These people have talked to us. They conducted a 30 day training about six or seven months ago, and if we're not working with them directly, then they are working in our subordinate units. We are in daily contact. We expect that this organisation will help us build up a military structure that will help us defend ourselves against any aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, maybe you can clear this up for me. Name one NATO corps, one corps in all of NATO that has 8.000 to 8.200, 8.000 to 8.200 troops? Name one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot name such a corps, but 8.000 to 8.200 soldiers under arms is the number of men under the organisation of men who were under arms in that area. This is what our strengths were. However, we had more soldiers. These were just people under arms. Take into consideration the area which we covered, which is about one third of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then you will arrive at the understanding of the facts as I presented them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift a little way away from NATO and move to the JNA and if I could hand out this exhibit with the permission of the Court. Mr. Dubuisson, our next number, if you will? I'm sorry, I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 476.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think we gave enough out there, because we have translations in both. Mr. President, I apologise, this is only in English and BSC, but I don't know if I gave Mr. Dubuisson enough copies. Here's an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 476, 476A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I use the English copy, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, the exhibit you have before you is a structure for the 4th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army and the 4th Corps had approximately 28.000 men in it, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that, the precise, I don't know what corps you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the 4th Corps in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, how many men were there in a corps in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall a corps, and again it would depend on the use that it was meant for, its task, you know, time of war. It would have 15.000 men and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, would you accept this 4th Corps had 28.000 men in it? Would you accept that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness just said that he does not know this corps or does not know how many men this corps had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Nobilo is right. You want him to say that the 4th Corps should have had 28.000 men. First of all, he is saying that he doesn't know and in general he is saying about 15.000 is the number they were. I know that's not the answer that you wanted, but move on to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge, we'll have other information on the size of this corps being 28.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many officers, junior officers and privates -- go to the last page -- what is the total in the headquarters of this 4th Corps? Count them up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the document that I have in front of me only makes reference to the command structure, not the entire size of the corps. It's clear from it that it had 91 commissioned officers, 20 non-commissioned and five just regular soldiers. That is what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, that, Brigadier, even if your numbers -- that is a staff, and my math may be wrong here, is 114, isn't it? For even by your estimate, 114 for even your estimate of approximately 15.000, there is 114 staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I, indeed, said that I do not know anything about the unit that this document refers to. I can only guess here. I can talk about these things in principle because for each --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have to intervene for a moment here, Mr. Kehoe. The Judges are here in order to serve as arbiters, but they do have to come in now and again because we're not having this man take a military examination within the context of NATO. Go to the point. You can't both show him a document that comes from you and then comes about figures saying, do you agree that? We can all do the addition as well and see that it adds up to 114. Try to go directly to your questions, Mr. Kehoe, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: According to this document, this document, Brigadier, the staff headquarters for the 4th Corps of the JNA on the 29th of August of 1991, had 114 personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He told you that he didn't know it. It's your document which says 114. We have to start with the figures on this document and that's all. Perhaps he should know. That's another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am only limiting my question to what this document reflects. This document reflects 114 personnel in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you're asking the witness whether he agrees with it or doesn't. That's what you have to do, does he agree with it or doesn't he? That's how I'd ask the question. Or I would ask him myself. Don't try to go around the bush, as it were. Go right to the point. I'll ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you agree with this document? In other words, the 4th Corps of the army of the 29 August, 1991, in your opinion, could it reasonably have had this number? It's an official document, that's the question that's being asked, you know or you don't know. That's all there is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not know how many men this corps had, but in this document, and we did our math all together it says 114, however, I cannot confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you said that the corps structure that you were familiar with in the JNA was approximately 15.000 men; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not how I said it. I said that the corps were different in size. They had different structures and the structure was defined by the task that this corps would have in wartime. For instance, you would not have the same kind of a corps in Vojvodina as you would in Bosnia. You would not establish a corps just for formality. It depends on the purposes, so we can talk about numbers and principle, but whether the number is 110, 114, indeed I cannot say either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, suffice to say, Brigadier, that in response to a question by Mr. Nobilo, you noted, and I am on page 12173 to 12174, that Blaskic in his headquarters needed 97 officers with a total personnel officers of 151; is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Question: Brigadier, according to the NATO standards, how many officers did Tihomir Blaskic need to have in order to carry out his duties? "Answer: If you look at the first row, first column, and you see the number of officers, he was supposed to have 97 active officers. That is a total of 151." Did you respond in that fashion to Mr. Nobilo's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, when asked a question regarding the structure of the command based on the NATO standards, I said that the number should have been 220. These numbers are referred to in the chart which I offered here. I don't know by heart whether it was 95 active duty officers, if I was to review these materials again, I would have given the same answer that I had given to Counsel Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, suffice to say that with 8.000 to 8.200 officers, your statement that Blaskic needed 97 officers and 151 total personnel in the headquarters is a gross exaggeration; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, either the interpretation is not good or I was misunderstood. My understanding was whether General Blaskic for 8.400 officers he needed 95 officers. But this is completely wrong because we never had 8.400 officers, so this may have been a misinterpretation. So if that was the case, please have the question asked again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps it was an interpretation problem. Because we're talking about 8.000 and then 200 officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel said 8.200 officers, we all listened, Mr. President, and waited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel, I appreciate that. It was a misspeak on my behalf and I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Please ask your questions clearly, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier for 8.000 to 8.200 soldiers which is what Mr. Zeco said was in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, your statement that Blaskic needed 97 officers and 151 total personnel in his headquarters is a gross exaggeration; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is no exaggeration and let me give you the reasons why: The Operative Zone command, when it was established and organised, had a task to produce a structure and an organisation for defence of the territory of Central Bosnia against the aggression of the army of Republika Srpska for 10 or 11 Brigades. This was our task, to create an organisation for that objective. In the last week I kept explaining all the time what we actually had on the ground. It is a fact that we did not have more than 8.500 men under arms, but we did have a larger number of men who were on our list. Now this is how it looked when we were holding a defence line, we had all the weapons and the defence line and the situation is worsening, the enemy is planning an attack. Then, what we would do, we would order the people that did not have the weapons to wait. This was maybe tragic, but they had to wait for somebody to get killed and then they would step inside the trench and pick up their weapon and keep on defending. The level of the command at the Operative Zone level, compared to NATO, the way we envisaged and the way our task was defined, this would have been at a level of a corps. But as we did not have artillery, armour and so on, we called ourselves an infantry corps. But when you say to an officer or a soldier, an infantry corps, he knows immediately what your size, what your force is and what this type of a corps can do, what it is capable of doing. I think that that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you told us that in the headquarters you had between 20 and 25 personnel; is that right? In the headquarters for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, between 23 and 25. It varied. If you were to ask me on a particular date, I would give you a specific figure, but the rough figure is not more than 25 and I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did it increase above 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was until the time of the Washington Agreement; it stayed at 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the war, from '92 until the end of '93, no, '92/'93, during the war, whether it was right up to the Washington Agreement, I wouldn't be able to say just now. I can't tell you right to the man, but during the war, '92, '93, we had up to 25 men in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This 477, A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, take a look at that document, if you could, while the Judges are taking a look at theirs and Defence counsel is taking a look at theirs. Take a look at this document, Brigadier, and I ask you to take a look at the last page. Do you recognise Colonel Blaskic's signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recognise that seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. It is the seal of the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Read, if you will, the items. You're welcome to read the entire document, I don't want to limit you in any fashion, but I'm basically directing my questions toward point number two. Tell me when you're through, Brigadier, and I will ask my next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were part of the staff on the 11th of August of 1993; were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in point two, about midway down in the first paragraph, Colonel Blaskic says that the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command is 59.4 per cent full with 38 posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, Your Honours, the figure 38 includes officers for communications, which we had formed, attached to the command of the Operative Zone, which was not originally envisaged; so that this number, the difference between the number I gave, that is 25 and 38, is due to this. So, this number includes communications officers, because we had international organisations, and that had not originally been envisaged, and we also had a press service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, drop four lines down, and it says Central Bosnia Operative Zone communication company, 19.6 per cent full with 22 members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, your statement to this Court that during the entire time you were in the headquarters, that the headquarters staff did not increase beyond 25 was inaccurate; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was accurate, because there were 25 persons directly working on the implementation of the orders of the commander, and in organising the work of the command, as regards combat and organisation in general. The people who were in the press service and who were in the department for communications, they were included in this total number, but they were working in another area, that is communications and the press service. This was not envisaged, according to our original structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me go back again to one of my questions I asked you previously on how many people should have been in that staff; in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone staff headquarters, if the staff was a hundred per cent filled, how many did you estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There should have been, according to our indicators that we had and the aim we set ourselves, there should have been about 105 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Blaskic himself, in the middle of the war, has 38 posts, according to him, that is 59 per cent full. My math may be incorrect, but if it's a hundred per cent filled, it would be 61; wouldn't it? By his own admission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could the question be even more precise for me to be able to answer it properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very simple, Brigadier. In this note that the accused sent to HVO main headquarters on the 11th of August 1993, in the middle of the war, he said that he had 38 posts filled, and that was 59.4 per cent filled. Do a quick approximate math calculation; if it was a hundred per cent filled, how many posts would he have filled in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone headquarters, 61, 62?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't work it out exactly, whether it's 61 or 62, but when I was talking about the structure Operative Zone command, I think we offered a document, and I would like us to have a look at that document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, we can look at any document you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is important for this witness to see the document, because it is from 1992 that envisaged a hundred men, and this is from August 1993; so, if we're making comparisons between the testimony in the direct examination and what the witness is saying now, we need to have the document so as to clear up the situation completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I gladly will take the time to give this witness the document, this is not meant to be any questioning that doesn't give this witness the opportunity to review any document he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with what you said, Mr. Kehoe. What is the document? What is the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would be perfectly honest with you, Judge, I read the document, but with 200 documents, I don't know the number. I think it was a 1992 document that was somewhat thick and had lists of positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo, do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Document D201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is one of the earliest ones, one of the first. Mr. Kehoe, so that everything is clear here, make things clear. What you want to do is make a comparison between a document which was signed by the accused, dated 18 November 1992, and D201, in which the accused, I don't know to whom he was writing to, but he said how the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command was supposed to be organised. You're comparing that document with the document you have just shown us, the A476, in which the accused makes a report to the central headquarters to say what posts he doesn't have, and then using the percentages you are trying to deduce, or you're trying to show that, to see whether or not there is a contradiction in what the witness said; is that correct, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, the witness asked to see 201, and my question is focused on 477, I took the position that if the witness wants to take a look at a prior Defence exhibit, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. We all agree about what we're talking about. Continue with your questions, please. Ask your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to look at exhibit 201, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, let me ask you a question, you said that your headquarter's staff was no more than 25, yet we see in this exhibit in August of 1993 that the headquarters staff went to a minimum of 38 posts; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that in the command there were 25 men. I repeat what I have already said. The difference shown in this report that you gave me, Mr. Kehoe, in relation to what I said, is attributable to the men who were working as communications officers. Because we don't have them mentioned here in the formation, as you can see. Then, also, people working in the press centre and the person who drafted this document included those men in the staff members of the Operative Zone command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you will agree with me, once again, that using the rough calculations of 59.4 per cent, Blaskic, in the middle of the war, told his headquarters in Mostar that if his posts were filled, that would amount to 62, 61, 62 posts in the headquarters. You would agree with me that that is what this document reflects.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The table that I was referring to when I spoke about the organisation and structure of the Operative Zone command is based on this document, which was tendered, I don't remember its number, under which number it was mapped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Document D201. In my testimony I gave information regarding the situation as it was, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The document speaks for itself, we will move on to another subject, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you mentioned that you had problems in the headquarters, because you said that not only did you not have enough people in the headquarters, but you didn't have enough trained people in the headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have enough trained officers with a military education, and also with military experience, I wish to emphasise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, my colleague reminded I'm going into another area. I don't know if this is a break time or if Your Honours want to keep going. I will gladly do anything Your Honours want me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you're going to change subjects, we'll take a 10 to 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you said were you going to change subjects now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am changing subjects, Your Honours, and I'm moving to the actual officer corps, both within the headquarters of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone and within the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the subject I will be moving to, Brigadier, and I move to that based on a statement you made, Brigadier, on page 12621, 12621, where you said that, "let me just remind you that in the brigade commands we did not have enough officers who had proper military training." Now, the first thing I would like to you do, Brigadier, if we could put this on the ELMO, and I believe it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Dubuisson, 80/ -- the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 80/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no D, it's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could, if we could somehow move the ELMO back closer to the Brigadier so he can point to things on the ELMO, it's a little difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you see that picture okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, just with the assistance of the usher, I don't know if there is a pointer there, I'm going to ask you to use a very sophisticated pointer, a chopstick, I think it is. No chopstick? Okay, a pen will suffice. Brigadier, take a look at that picture, you see the accused, Colonel Blaskic, in the middle of that; don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who is seated on the Colonel's right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Filipovic, General Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General Filipovic, after General Blaskic became a Brigadier in the HVO, took over the Central Bosnia area for the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After General Blaskic was appointed Chief of Staff of the main headquarters of the HVO, General Filipovic became commander of the Vitez Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When he was in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, and when Colonel Blaskic was the commander, what role did Colonel Filipovic have, or now General Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Filipovic, after Travnik fell that is, after units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina pushed back the HVO from Travnik, at that time General Filipovic, as far as I can recall, had certain duties in the joint command, I think together with General Arif Pasalic, I'm not quite sure of that. So, after the fall of Travnik, after the joint command ceased to function because of the overall attack by the BH army against the HVO in the Lasva Valley and beyond, General Filipovic in August or September, as far as I remember, was deputy commander of the Vitez military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was General Filipovic prior to joining the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Filipovic was a former officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What rank did he hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was a lieutenant colonel, I'm not quite sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was an active JNA officer at the time he left the JNA and joined the HVO; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To the colonel's, talking of Colonel's Blaskic's left, who is that gentleman? Point to him, if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the left of Colonel Blaskic is Franjo Nakic, Chief of Staff of the Vitez military district, or the Vitez Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was Franjo Nakic's military experience prior to joining the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Franjo Nakic graduated from the school for reserve officers in the same way that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what rank did he hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Franjo Nakic, I'm not sure exactly what rank he had. I think it was captain first class, or major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to a Defence exhibit, and that is exhibit 251, and if we could put that on the ELMO. Can you see that, Brigadier? Can you see that document clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it, but I can't read the text, the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have an extra copy -- we do have an extra copy, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you see that okay, Brigadier? Heaven knows I couldn't see it without glasses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at the brigade structure on the bottom of this particular document. In April of 1993 there are two brigades in Travnik that are missing; is that right, that are not on this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Travnik Brigade, I can see it on the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm talking about the Zenica brigades. I apologise, I misspoke again. Counsel just said it was a space problem, there's two missing. I just want to talk about the two missing, first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Zenica brigade, Jure Francetic Brigade is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade in April 1993 was Zivko Totic, today a Brigadier, who was abducted by BH army members, whose escort was killed, and the brigade commander was taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now Brigadier Totic, what was his military experience prior to joining the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, Brigadier Totic had completed a higher military school, section engineers, and specifically he was working on engineering works at airports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He, at the time he left the JNA, was an active officer in the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there was another brigade in Zenica, and that was the 2nd Zenica Brigade, whose commander was Vinko Baresic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second Zenica brigade never functioned properly, the command of the Operative Zone wanted to establish and organise that brigade, but the conflicts prevented us from achieving that goal. The commander that you mentioned, Mr. Vinko Baresic, did, indeed, have the duty of establishing that brigade as the commander; but that brigade was never properly organised because of the war that broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When the war broke out, or when the HVO was formed, Vinko Baresic was also an active officer in the JNA as well; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Vinko Baresic completed the school for reserve officers, and he worked in the district TO staff for, in the department for information and propaganda, or rather for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, he was an officer that had gone to reserve officer's school, like you and Franjo Nakic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to the Bobovac Brigade, and the Bobovac Brigade was commanded by a gentleman by the name of Emil Harah; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emil Harah. However, the commander of that brigade changed; so, I couldn't tell you exactly when the brigade commanders were on duty at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you know Emil Harah; do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Emil Harah in 1992 when I visited the command of that brigade at Ponikve, and we met officially then. I'm not familiar with his biography, or his career, or what he did before the war. After the war, after the attack of the BH army on Vares, Emil Harah, as far as I know, fled to join the army of Republika Srpska, and after that I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was Emil Harah an active JNA officer prior to joining the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was not, but I'm not sure of that, because I said that I knew the man for only two or three months. I went there, the war broke out, he went over to the army of Republika Srpska, so I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's keep going on this list, and the next one on the chart is the Viteska Brigade, which you testified was formed in March of 1993, and whose commander was Mario Cerkez. What military training did Mario Cerkez have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez had a regular education, secondary school, and he also completed the school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as you stated previously, this is the school for reserve officers that was an intricate part of the JNA defence system in the former Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school for reserve officers lasted six months, the training lasted six months. The programme of training lasted six months, and this was within the framework of regular military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move down the line on this chart, and we'll go to the 111th Zepce Brigade, whose commander was Ivo Lovancic. Do you see it on the chart there, the 111th Zepce Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, the 111th XP Brigade. The commander was Ivo Lozancic, as far as I know. I think you said Livancic, maybe it's a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Brigadier, I'm not essentially fluent with the names, and if I make a mistake, bear with me. Lozancic I'm sure is the right pronunciation, and I wouldn't want to quibble with you about that. Nevertheless, what is the military experience of Ivo Lozancic of the 111th Zepce Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think that Mr. Lozancic hadn't even completed the school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to learn that he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I wasn't sure whether he had or not, so I can't claim anything. Because I didn't have much contact with Lozancic, because we were cut off in the period from '92 and throughout 1993, I was in Zepce only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go down the list to Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak. We had a couple of commanders for the Bonn Jelacic Brigade; didn't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the functions of commander were performed by two people, one was Mijo Bozic and then Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us about Mijo Bozic, and he graduated from the military academy in the former JNA, and he was an active officer in the JNA prior to joining the HVO; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mijo Bozic did graduate from the military academy, and he held a position in the district staff of the Territorial Defence in Zenica. He was one of the assistants, I think, for intelligence work or something like that, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the other gentleman about whom we heard some testimony who was a commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, Ivica Rajic. He was an active officer in the JNA before joining the HVO, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met Mr. Lozancic when we were establishing the defence line towards Travnik. As far as I remember, Mr. Rajic completed secondary military school. I don't exactly know which branch, but secondary military school and not military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was he an active officer in the JNA before he joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this is an example of an officer who didn't go to the military academy, but became an active officer in the HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you be more precise in your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic did not go to the military academy, but he was an active officer in the JNA, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's keep going down to the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade, the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade. Who was the commander of the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall the name. I visited the Commander of that Brigade once. I think it was a person called Neven and he was a corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you recognise the name of Slavko Zelic, Z-e-l-i-c?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me make sure I don't make a mistake. The Kralj Tvrtko Brigade. I got confused. You're talking about the Sarajevo Brigade. I'm sorry, I made an error. I did not know any of the officers in the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade because I was never able to visit the Commander of that Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough. How about the next Brigade that's in that list and it's the Brigade in Busovaca, the Nikola Subic Zrinski Brigade? Whose Commander was Dusko Grubisic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was Dusko Grubisic's military background before becoming a Brigade Commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Grubisic didn't have any military education. Within the framework of his general education, he had a three-year secondary school for qualified work as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that Dusko Grubisic did not go to reserve officer school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going on that list. The -- -- and pardon my pronunciation -- the Kotromanic Brigade and that's in Kakanj. And Mr. Maric was the Commander there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the name Neven, but also because we were cut off, I visited the Commander of this Brigade only once on my way back from Vares in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So do you have any knowledge as to his military experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, in the former JNA, he had the rank of lieutenant. This is a young officer who has only just graduated from the academy. I don't know whether he was active for a year or two, I cannot say, because I didn't personally know the mentioned Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Mr. Maric also graduated from the JNA academy for the former JNA before he became an officer in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure when talking about the Commander of the Kakanj Brigade whether he had graduated from the academy or not, but I think he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, he certainly was an active JNA officer before he joined the HVO, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pardon me, Brigadier, didn't you just say that Mr. Marin was a lieutenant -- excuse me, Mr. Neven Maric was a lieutenant in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that as far as I can recall, but I am not sure, he was a lieutenant, and if he was a lieutenant, that means he graduated from the military academy. I visited the Commander of this Brigade once. Because we were cut off, I couldn't visit that Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's move down the list here to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik. Who was the Commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik was Zeljko Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his military background before he joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Sabljic had graduated from the academy for reserve officers, and he specialised in electrical engineering, and he was never an active service officer of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about the Travnik Brigade and Jozo Leutar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Jozo Leutar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again pardon my pronunciation Brigadier. Do you know Mr. Leutar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Mr. Leutar when he assumed the duty of the Commander of the Travnik Brigade. As far as I know, he was an official in the Ministry of the Interior before the war. I am not sure whether he had any military training before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a reserve officer, had gone through the reserve officer training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not have been that if you had not had any reserve officer training, which took about six months to complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in your opinion, Mr. Leutar did go to the reserve officer training school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that and I do not know this. I only know that before the war, Mr. Leutar worked in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's move down another notch in the strata within these Brigade structures and the HVO, and let's talk about the military experience that is off the chart that's before you, and talk about some of the officer corps in these various Brigades that we've been discussing. Let's start with the 111th Zepce Brigade, the 111th XP Brigade. And pardon my pronunciation again here, Brigadier, but do you know Drago Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Drago Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he a member in the 111th Zepce Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please ask a more specific question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was he a Commander for the HVO in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In any time period. Was he ever an officer in the JNA? Any kind of a Commander of a Brigade, of a Battalion, anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Drago Dragicevic did not graduate from a military academy, so, in other words, he was not an officer of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he go to the reserve officer training school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to another officer that is in the headquarters, Ivica Cobanac. Do you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know Mr. Cobanac. He was in the Operative Zone command and, as far as I know, he was there for about two or three months and then he was transferred to another duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was he transferred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can just further clarify this, during 1993, Brigadier Cobanac did not work in the Operative Zone command, but he was Commander of a company in Sebesic, which was his birth place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When was Mr. Cobanac in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say the precise time frame, but I know that this was during 1992. This was in '92. Just a moment, let me try to remember. So that would be '92, towards the end, and occasionally he would come in early 1993. He would come from Sebesic of his birth place he would come to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now he graduated from the JNA military academy just like Colonel Blaskic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he graduated from a military college, which was a two-year military school. I believe that he was a Commander, a platoon Commander in the former Yugoslav People's Army and his rank, I think was lieutenant, which is the lowest commission officer rank in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, would it surprise you that Mr. Cobanac was a captain when he left the JNA and joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised because I never looked at his personal file. I am just speaking on the basis of what he told me because after '95, we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, just let's recapitulate something you just noted for the Court. So, in addition to active officers in the JNA, many have gone to the military academy like the accused, and they had reserve officers. There was also a two-year military college for officers in the JNA as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the one that Mr. Cobanac went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is what he graduated from. This is what he told me. Again, I did not see his personal file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in the OP zone command in Vitez was Franjo Gojsilovic, pardon my pronunciation, Gojsilovic, Goj, G-o-j-s-i-l-o-v-i-c?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that name. Could you perhaps describe his position so I may recall. But the name that you just mentioned, I just do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it past the fact that my pronunciation on this subject, Brigadier, is something less than accurate. Nevertheless, was a gentleman by the name of Franjo in operations and training body within the OP zone headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know him, but I know that there were two men by the name of Franjo in the OP zone command. Later on, maybe even up to four. But there were two, there were Franjo Nakic and Franjo Slikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I may have written the name wrong. Brigadier, we'll pass on this Franjo and move to Ivica Miskovic in the Viteska Brigade. Do you know that gentleman? Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Miskovic in the Vitez Brigade, can you perhaps tell me what duty he was on? Because there were a lot of changes in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was in the Vitez Brigade. He was an officer in the Vitez Brigade. He had been a reserve officer. Had gone to reserve officer school and was a lieutenant officer in the former JNA and during the war he was in the Viteska Brigade under Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you specify the time frame? You know why, because I would go to help out in the Viteska Brigade and I then got to know this man. This was in 1993. It was in November/December. This was to help out after the Krizanicevo Selo was attacked by the BH army and we had a lot of losses, so we had to give them assistance. During that period, I did not meet this person. However, if I knew the exact time frame and the duty, then I may be able to provide you an answer. But as you pronounce this name, I really cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't blame you, Brigadier. We'll move to another name. Marinko and I am not going to pronounce this name correctly, Ljoyjo, L-j-o-y-j-o, in the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak Brigade, are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marinko Ljoyjo I did meet, and this was after the Washington Agreement. I met him at the Kupres front-line during the last operations for the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not know exactly what duty he was on during the war because Kiseljak was cut off. I know far fewer people that in a case of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Busovaca and Vitez formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, had he been a reserve officer in the JNA prior to joining the HVO holding the rank of lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that with respect to Marinko Ljoyjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about Igor Bosnjak? Do you know Mr. Bosnjak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What Brigade is he from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He worked in your headquarters, sir. Igor Bosnjak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you specify the duty?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was in charge of IPD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that name. I am not aware of this person being in the OP zone headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. We'll move back to the Viteska Brigade, Alojz Gasparovic. Are you familiar with an officer in the Viteska Brigade by the name of Gasparovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Zeljko, and this is the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade from Novi Travnik, your hometown, Zeljko Sablec, S-a-b-l-e-c? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Sablec was Commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. I had said that he had graduated from the reserve officers training school, specialising in engineering. I know that he worked in the Bratsko company and that's all I know. He lived in the town of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, within that Brigade, sir, Ilija Marin, also in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, are you familiar with Mr. Marin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Marin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he a captain in the -- a reserve captain in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Marin was not in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not in the former JNA. But are you asking me whether he was an active duty person? Was he in reserves? If you can specify the question so I can give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am asking you whether or not Mr. Marin, like you and like so many others, went to the reserve officers training school for the former JNA and held the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Marin did go to the reserve officers training school, which lasted for six months. He was a reserve captain. He had a rank of the reserve captain. As far as I recall, in this former Territorial Defence, he was a company Commander. This is what we were trained for in this school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to the Travnik Brigade, if I may, sir. And you said you know officers in the Travnik Brigade and Novi Travnik Brigade, the Vitez Brigade. Dario Sucic, S-u-c-i-c, of the Travnik Brigade, do you know Mr. Sucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Dario Sucic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's probably what I mean, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know Dario Sucic. He, as far as I know, went to the secondary military school and specialised in communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he an active officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not an active service officer. He was a junior officer. In other words, he was a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was a non-commissioned officer in the JNA; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This in NATO it is non-commissioned officers. In local nomenclature, it's junior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right. As a junior officer, was he an active junior officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did he do in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the chief of communications in the Travnik Brigade. Later, until 1995, he changed his posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us shift gears and go down Busovaca, Brigadier, and let's talk about the Nikola Subic Zrnski Brigade and Jure Cavara. Are you familiar with Mr. Cavara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Jure Cavara?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again, probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Jure Cavara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he a reserve officer in the JNA as well, holding the rank of lieutenant or was he a captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Jure did graduate from the reserve officer training school. I do not know his exact rank as reserve officer. From the civilian education, I believe that he had some kind of a secondary school of economics, at least that is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let's go down to Kiseljak and talk about a Commander down there by the name of Mario Bradara, do you know Mr. Bradara, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Bradara, we met during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He still carries a rank in the armed forces, does he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
